--- Page 1 ---
Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling
of AI Data Center Tasks
Xin Qin, Dawei Qiu
School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering
Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
{xin.qin, dawei.qiu}@ntu.edu.sg
Fei Teng
Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering
Imperial College London, London, UK
f.teng@imperial.ac.uk
Abstract—AI data centers receive computing tasks continu-
ously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and
electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges
this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule
inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start
period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational
constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while
keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100
GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed
rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling
tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization
benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no
solver, much less computation time.
Index
Terms—AI
data
center,
demand
flexibility,
online
scheduling, GPU workload, real-time electricity price.
I. INTRODUCTION
A. Background
AI data centers (AIDCs), which host training and infer-
ence clusters, are now large electrical loads, and electricity
has become their largest operating expense, accounting for
about two-thirds of the operating cost [1]. Their cost is also
increasingly exposed to wholesale prices, which vary within
the day. To reduce energy cost, part of their workload can be
shifted to low-price periods by delays of minutes to hours, and
experiments on GPU clusters have shown power reductions
without compromising service targets [2], [3]. These findings
motivate scheduling the start times of delay-tolerant tasks to
exploit lower-price periods while still completing every task.
The difficulty is a mismatch between the timescales of
computing and energy. On the computing side, tasks arrive
continuously, time-stamped to the second [4]. On the energy
side, electricity is bought day ahead or in real time priced
per hour or per 15 min, and an energy optimization that
decides task start periods requires computational resources and
time. This creates a dilemma: If the AIDC operator solves the
optimization whenever a task arrives, the solver may not finish
before the next arrival; If the operator solves it once per period
instead, tasks wait unnecessarily for the next solve and may
miss low-price periods.
This paper therefore address one question: Can a solver-free
rule that schedules each task once, on arrival, respect the GPU
and CPU capacities while optimizing energy cost?
B. Literature Review
Existing works on energy-aware task scheduling in data
centers follow three approaches.
First, horizon-based methods plan a given workload over
a given horizon. For example, the method in [5] uses day-
ahead carbon forecasts to cap the next day’s hourly capacity
for flexible workloads. Recent AIDC studies schedule training
and inference workloads by robust optimization under uncer-
tainty [6] or by a MILP for an AIDC operating as a microgrid
prosumer [7]. These methods suit advance scheduling, when
all tasks and prices are known, but are difficult to apply in
real time as tasks arrive.
Second, online methods decide each job as it arrives.
Paper [8] delays flexible tasks into the lowest-carbon period
within a waiting limit, also considering cloud service cost.
Work [9] schedules tasks slot by slot under stochastic prices,
and work [10] proposes a randomized online job and energy
optimizer with a competitive ratio, building on online allo-
cation theory [11], [12]. These rules target carbon, service
cost or worst-case guarantees, rather than the energy cost
minimization under resource limits.
Third, multi-timescale methods separate fast and slow de-
cisions. Work [13] switches servers on a slow time scale and
sets service rates every slot, with Lyapunov bounds on cost and
delay. Work [14] shapes the load one day ahead and places
arriving jobs in real time, and D3T [15] assigns queued tasks to
different sites at a time scale of seconds and optimizes cooling
every 30 min. These methods decide where a task runs or how
fast queued work is served, which may rely on offline training,
however, they do not decide when flexible tasks start to reduce
energy costs.
C. Contributions
This paper proposes an online optimization method that
schedules AIDC tasks in real time. We take the perspective
of the AIDC operator, as a price-taker, and schedule the
tasks submitted during an operating day as they arrive. The
contributions are summarized below:
1) A fast online scheduling method. The proposed method
decides each task once, at submission, by choosing its start
period within the allowed delay, and achieves high computa-
tional efficiency without a solver.
2) A cost-efficient rule based on dual decomposition. In-
spired by dual decomposition, the proposed method integrates
the CPU/GPU resource shadow prices and reserves capacity,
which contributes to cost optimization and keeps high-priority
tasks on time.

practical AI task data in the A100 GPU trace, we investigate
the operational cost and computation time of the proposed
method by comparing it with an energy-unaware rule, a multi-
timescale optimization, and the perfect offline optimum.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion II introduces the problem setting and formulation. Sec-
tion III proposes the online rule. Section IV presents case
studies and comparisons with benchmarks, and Section V
presents conclusions and discussion.
II. MODEL FORMULATION
We introduce the model formulation in this section. For
clarity, we list the notation in Table I.
A. Problem setting and assumptions
We take the perspective of an AIDC operator who receives
computing tasks and aims to minimize its energy cost as a
price taker. The AIDC is exposed to the prices of a two-
settlement wholesale market, as in the US or China, either
directly or through a retailer that passes these prices on. The
day-ahead and real-time prices over period t are denoted by
λDA
t
and λRT
t
, respectively. The operator schedules tasks in
operation periods t ∈T of length ∆t, the interval at which
it makes decisions, which ranges from seconds to minutes.
On-site generations and the adjustment of cooling are not
considered. Tasks submitted before the operating day are
already running; together with the idle power, they form the
day-ahead schedule, settled at λDA
t
. We focus on the tasks
submitted during the operating day, which need to schedule in
real time. Their energy is a deviation from day-ahead schedule
and is settled at λRT
t
.
Tasks can be submitted at any second, and every task should
be completed. Task j is submitted at sj, runs for ℓj (spanning
nj = ⌈ℓj/∆t⌉periods), and requests rG
j GPUs and rC
j vCPUs.
It can start from period tj, the first period that begins at or after
sj, and may wait up to Dj further periods. Tasks are divided
into two categories: 1) High-priority (HP) tasks, such as online
inference, are inflexible and start without delay (Dj = 0); 2)
Flexible tasks, such as model training and batch inference,
can wait up to Dj periods. Once a task is scheduled, its start
cannot be postponed: a user who has been told that a task will
finish within the next hour would not accept it finishing two
hours later because of the operator’s scheduling.
B. Optimization problem formulation
The AIDC operator minimizes the real-time cost of the tasks
submitted during the day over a horizon of T periods. Given
all tasks and prices, the offline schedule solves the following
mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem:

--- Page 3 ---
∆t gives each task more start periods, and hence more binary
variables, so the MILP may not be solved within one period.
Overall, problem (1)–(3) minimizes the real-time energy
cost. Since Cj,t is a constant, the problem is linear in x and
is a MILP, with integrality only through xj,t ∈{0, 1}.
III. SOLUTION METHOD
The formulation in (1)–(3) cannot be applied directly during
operation for three reasons. First, tasks arrive one at a time, so
in period t only the tasks submitted so far are known, and the
global optimum cannot be obtained without the complete task
information. Second, the AIDC operator’s decision every ∆t
(by solving a MILP over the waiting tasks) may not be finished
within a period of seconds, but solving it less often, e.g. every
15 min, makes arriving tasks wait for the next solve. Third,
the real-time price is known only for the current settlement
interval, so later prices must be forecast.
To address these limits, we propose a solver-free online
rule that assigns each task a start period upon arrival while
respecting GPU and CPU capacity constraints. The workflow
of the proposed method is illustrated in Fig. 1.
A. Online Scheduling Rule
This section presents the proposed online rule, which sched-
ules the tasks of problem (1)–(3) as they arrive. Each task
is scheduled once, at its submission time sj, in order of
submission.
Expected cost: A task submitted at sj can run from period
tj onward. With the forecast of real-time prices denoted by
ˆλt, for a task j, the expected cost of starting it in period t is

solves (1)–(3). If capacity binds, the optimal µc
t is finite and
assigns a congested period to the task that gains most from it,
whereas (12) assigns it to the first arrival.

IV. CASE STUDY
A. Case Setup
We consider the operation of a AIDC cluster located in
California, US. It has 3,456 A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs and
55,296 vCPUs. Each GPU draws 50 W when idle and 400 W
at full load, and each vCPU 1 W and 5 W. With a PUE of
ρ = 1.30, the facility power ranges from 297 kW with all
servers idle to 2,157 kW at full load.
We consider that the AIDC is exposed to CAISO wholesale
prices, including two parts: The day-ahead part, for the idle
power and the tasks already running from the previous day,
and the real-time part, for the tasks submitted during the
operating day. We focus on the real-time part. We use the
NP15 locational marginal prices of August 21, 2026 (Fig. 2).
The tasks come from the job set of the reference [4], which
records the submission time, duration and GPU and CPU
requests of each job. We make two changes for our tests.
First, we reassign each job to one of three priority classes,
HP, Priority and Spot, while keeping its other features. Second,
to stress the capacity logic, we move jobs recorded on other
GPU types into the considered task set, so that peak demand
reaches about 109.2% of GPU capacity while all tasks can
still be completed within the horizon.
On the operating day, 1,622 tasks from yesterday are already
running at 00:00, and 1,343 new tasks are submitted during
the day (350 HP, 311 Priority and 682 Spot), which may arrive
at any second, as shown in Fig. 3.
We compare four cases: 1) Proposed: the solver-free online
rule; 2) Benchmark 1 (earliest feasible): starts each task in
its earliest feasible period without considering energy cost;
3) Benchmark 2 (rolling MILP): re-solves (1)–(3) for waiting
tasks at each update every 5 min (following multi-timescale
dispatch); and 4) Perfect (offline MILP): solves the full-
horizon problem (1)–(3) after the day with all tasks and
prices known, providing a perfect-information reference with
the global optimum. For a fair comparison of computation

The simulation settings are summarized in Table II.
B. Cost and Computation
Table III shows the energy cost and scheduling performance
of flexible tasks (only Priority and Spot). Benchmark 1 starts
each task in its earliest feasible period. The proposed method
instead delays Priority and Spot tasks by 18.9 and 39.1 min
on average, shifting them to lower-price periods. This lowers
the flexible-task cost by $37.28 (9.9%). The proposed method
also costs $0.53 (0.16%) less than Benchmark 2. Although
this saving is modest, Benchmark 2 has three drawbacks: 1)
it takes over 1,000 times longer per decision compared to
the proposed method; 2) since it updates only every 5 min,
tasks wait 1.2 min longer on average; and 3) with no capacity
reserved for HP tasks, seven HP tasks start late, violating their
timing requirements. (We did not add penalty in the reported
cost.) Finally, the proposed method costs $5.77 (1.7%) more
than Perfect. However, Perfect requires complete knowledge
of future tasks and prices and takes 52.8 s (nearly 1 min)
to solve the full-horizon problem, making it impractical for
real-time operation.
C. Capacity and HP Tasks
GPU capacity is the binding constraint: utilization reaches
100% around 03:00, 10:00–12:00 and 17:00–19:00 under the
proposed method (Fig. 4), while vCPU utilization remains
below 97% across all methods (Fig. 5). Both the proposed
method and Benchmark 1 reserve capacity for future HP tasks
and start all HP tasks on time. However, Benchmark 1 does
not consider the impact of electricity prices, leaving GPU load
high during the high-price periods around 09:00 and 19:00
(Fig. 4), whereas the proposed method combines capacity
reservation with price-aware scheduling. Benchmark 2 also
uses price forecasts but lacks capacity reservation. Earlier
batches can therefore occupy the available GPU capacity,
delaying seven HP tasks by 5–32 min.


--- Page 5 ---
Fig. 4. GPU use per period of the four cases.
Fig. 5. vCPU use per period of the four cases.
D. Impact of the Price and Task Forecast
On the operating day, the day-ahead price follows the shape
of the real-time price (Fig. 2), so it serves as a reasonable
forecast. The proposed method and Benchmark 2 use the same
information: the day-ahead price as the price forecast, and
perfect knowledge of the HP arrivals.
With capacity mostly slack, µc
t = 0 in most periods, so both
methods take the cheapest start under the forecast, and their
hourly costs differ by at most $0.6 (Fig. 6). The gap to Perfect
comes from forecast error: between 12:00 and 17:00, the real-
time price falls 9–19 $/MWh below the day-ahead price, so
Perfect shifts load from 09:00–12:00 to 12:00–16:00 (Fig. 7).
From 17:00, when the forecast matches the price, the hourly
costs agree within $1. This shows the value of better price
forecasts.
V. CONCLUSION
In this work, we propose an online solver-free rule that
schedules each task of an AIDC once, at submission, in its
cheapest capacity-feasible start period under the forecast real-
time price, given the day-ahead schedule. Under a stressed
workload, the proposed method has a 9.9% lower cost than the
earliest-feasible rule (Benchmark 1). Compared with a rolling
MILP (Benchmark 2), it achieves a slightly lower cost, starts
all HP tasks on time, and needs 0.024 ms per decision against
41.4 ms per update. Its cost is within 1.7% of the perfect
offline optimum. Future work will address task and market
price uncertainty, multi-day evaluations, and the theoretical
bound of the online algorithm.
